item.title: AGIBOT introduces Worken to measure robot productivity at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
AGIBOT unveiled its AHA3 integrated platform, GO-3 Preview, and WITA-Omni 1.0 model, as well as the G2 Max robot and Link-U OS 1.0 framework.

The post AGIBOT introduces Worken to measure robot productivity at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026 appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Peng Zhihui, president, CTO, and director of AGIBOT, introduces Worken at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026. Source: AGIBOT

AGIBOT today introduced Worken, a proposed framework for measuring the productivity of robots in real-world environments, at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026 in Shanghai. Combining the words “Work” and “Token,” the concept seeks to shift attention beyond the number of robots manufactured or deployed toward how much useful work they can perform autonomously and consistently.

The company also unveiled AHA3, its integrated “three intelligences in one” hardware platform, and highlighted advances in its AGILE motion intelligence framework, including a new self-evolving agent capability. AGIBOT debuted GO-3 Preview, its next-generation embodied AI foundation model, showcased its WITA-Omni 1.0 omni-modal interaction model, and launched the G2 Max industrial robot and Link-U OS 1.0.

The event also featured actual applications across manufacturing and commercial services, demonstrating AGIBOT’s focus on translating robotics innovation into productive work. The company said they reflect its deployment-first focus, with practical innovation spanning robot hardware, locomotion, task and interaction intelligence, operations, and an ecosystem intended to support real-world deployment at scale.

Founded in 2023 as Zhiyuan Xinchuang Technology Co., AGIBOT is focused on embodied AI. The Shanghai-based company‘s portfolio spans humanoid robots, quadrupeds, dexterous systems, and commercial cleaning systems. Last month, AGIBOT said its 20,000th robot had rolled off the production line, and IDC reported that the company led global humanoid robot shipments in the first half of 2026.

Submit your innovation now!

Worken is a proposed measure of robot productivity

As robots move from large-scale production into increasingly diverse applications, AGIBOT said there is another dimension of progress: the productive work robots can deliver once deployed. In addition to manufacturing scale, technological capabilities, and deployment milestones, the company said sustained autonomous operation and measurable task output are increasingly important indicators of robotic value.

“Over the past few years, the robotics industry has made remarkable progress in hardware, AI models, and large-scale manufacturing,” stated Peng Zhihui, co-founder, president, and chief technology officer of AGIBOT. “But as robots begin working in factories, warehouses, and service environments, we need to answer a more practical question: How much productive work are they actually delivering?”

“Worken is our attempt to develop a new way of answering that question,” he added. “We want to move beyond measuring how many robots are built or delivered and begin measuring how effectively they can perform useful work, autonomously and consistently, in the real world.”

Even deployments involving similar numbers of robots can deliver different levels of productivity, depending on how independently the machines operate, how frequently human intervention is required and how much acceptable work they complete.

AGIBOT described Worken as “effective intelligent work hours,” bringing three factors into a proposed measurement framework:

Worken = Number of Active Robots × Autonomous Working Hours × Output Efficiency Ratio

The first factor counts robots actively performing tasks in real-world environments, rather than units simply manufactured or held in inventory. The second measures time spent working autonomously, rather than total powered-on time.

The third factor assesses productive output against a reference benchmark for a defined task, such as the amount of acceptable work completed by a human worker under established operating standards.

The Worken framework combines the number of active robots, autonomous working hours, and an output efficiency ratio to measure robot productivity in real-world deployments. Source: AGIBOT

By connecting deployment scale, autonomy, and task output in Worken, AGIBOT said it wants to provide a more comprehensive way to describe robotic productivity across applications such as industrial handling, logistics, inspection, and commercial services.

“The concept also opens up a broader discussion about the economics of robotics,” said the company. “While hardware depreciates over time, improvements in software and AI models may enable the same machine to perform more useful work during its operating life. Measuring that output alongside total lifecycle costs could help businesses evaluate the longer-term value of robotic deployments.”

AGIBOT said Worken is an evolving framework that will be further refined through deployments and operational data. By developing task-specific benchmarks and accumulating practical experience across different applications, the company said it hopes that Worken can serve as a widely applicable reference for measuring the productive value of physical AI.

The event also featured the release of the “2026 Embodied Intelligence Industry Innovation Report,” which discussed the industry’s progress toward real-world deployment. Jointly compiled by China Economic Information Service and the Shanghai Industrial Innovation Center of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT), the report included Worken and AGIBOT’s deployment examples as part of its industry analysis.

AGIBOT unveils AHA3 platform and new physical AI models

The AGIBOT Humanoid Architecture, or AHA3, which unifies “three intelligences in one” — locomotion, interaction, and manipulation Intelligence — in an embodied AI system. The company said it designed the third-generation hardware architecture to improve efficiency.

Built on advances in motor-drive technology, integrated computing, and high-speed connectivity including Wi-Fi 6 and 5G, the AHA3 is designed to reduce integration complexity, improve system responsiveness, and support more capable robots in industrial applications.

To support sustained industrial deployment, AGIBOT also introduced a joint liquid-cooling system intended to improve thermal performance during continuous operation, alongside specialized joints with IP67-rated protection for more demanding environments.

Zhihui shows a hardware component of the AHA3 platform at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026.

AGILE advances locomotion

AGIBOT showed advances in its AGILE “multimodal, end-to-end locomotion intelligence” framework. The architecture spans general-purpose motion foundation models, generative motion control, integrated whole-body perception and control, and a newly introduced self-evolving agent capability.

AGILE is designed to enable robots to explore the boundaries of their physical capabilities and progressively improve their performance through experience, extending motion intelligence beyond predefined behaviors toward greater autonomy and adaptability.

AGIBOT described the framework as “a shift from motion control toward spatial mobility intelligence, with the goal of helping robots adapt to the layouts and changing conditions of real deployment sites.”

A demonstration of task execution with GO-3 Preview, an embodied AI foundation model integrating reasoning, prediction, and action. Source: AGIBOT

MEgo Glove and OmniHand get hands-on experience

On the data side, AGIBOT introduced MEgo Glove, a wearable tactile data-collection device designed to capture human hand movements and contact information for training embodied AI models.

Offered in Air and Ultra versions, the glove supports finger-pose capture, while the Ultra version adds three-dimensional fingertip and palm force data and torque information. The system is intended to help turn hands-on work experience into training data that can support robots after deployment.

In addition, AGIBOT’s new dexterous hand family includes OmniHand 3 Lite, OmniHand 3 and OmniHand 3 Ultra, as well as the OmniPicker 3 tactile gripper, expanding the options for fine manipulation and task-specific deployment.

The OmniHand robotic end effectors are designed for dexterous manipulation. Source: AGIBOT

GO-3 Preview is built around WRAM

AGIBOT also debuted GO-3 Preview, a next-generation embodied foundation model built around a World Reasoning Action Model (WRAM). The framework is designed to help robots anticipate the consequences of their actions, adapt to changing environments, and generalize beyond previously learned task sequences.

The company also demonstrated zero-shot and few-shot capabilities and presented its approach to “physical intelligence scaling,” which combines pre-training and post-training with continuous improvement after deployment. This approach aims to enable robots to expand their capabilities through both structured training and experience gained from real-world operations.

AGIBOT also highlighted GO-3 Preview’s benchmark performance. According to evaluation results presented at the event, the model ranked first in both task success rate and process score on RoboDojo, achieved the highest overall score on RoboTwin, and ranked first in overall score on RoboColiseum.

These results demonstrate the model’s performance across multiple evaluation frameworks covering robotic manipulation and task execution. Across task and interaction intelligence, AGIBOT is seeking to connect data, models, robot hardware, and operating scenarios across pre-training, post-training, deployment and day-to-day operations. Feedback from real tasks can then inform subsequent improvements to models and workflows, creating a deployment-driven data flywheel.

Dr. Yao Maoqing, co-founder, executive director, co-president, and president of the embodied AI business at AGIBOT, explains how GO-3 Preview and feedback from real-world deployments support the company’s data–model–robot–scenario learning loop. Source: AGIBOT

WITA-Omni 1.0 integrates features for human-robot interaction

For human-robot interaction, AGIBOT showcased WITA-Omni 1.0, an omni-modal foundation model that integrates visual perception, speech, real-time dialogue, facial expressions, and physical actions into a continuous interaction system.

The model supports full-duplex conversation, coordinated speech and movement, and on-device deployment, enabling more natural and responsive communication in complex environments. WITA-Omni 1.0 currently ranks first on multiple benchmarks related to embodied interaction, including Daily-Omni.

AGIBOT said AHA3, AGILE, GO-3 Preview and WITA-Omni 1.0 reflect its progress across integrated hardware architecture, locomotion intelligence, task execution and human-robot interaction. The company is also expanding its data collection, simulation and training capabilities through initiatives including AGIBOT WORLD 2026, the MEgo product family and Genie Sim 3.0, supporting the continued development of its physical AI models. This week, it also launched Genie Studio 2.0.

Xiong Yan, partner, executive director, co-president, president of central R&D, and president of the interaction business at AGIBOT, presents WITA-Omni 1.0 and its planned deployment roadmap for more natural, multimodal human–robot interaction. Source: AGIBOT

AGIBOT Launches G2 Max

AGIBOT launched G2 Max, a heavy-duty industrial robot designed for manufacturing and logistics applications. Featuring 21 degrees of freedom, a dual-arm handling capacity of up to 40 kg (88 lb.) and an adjustable working height ranging from 0.1 to 2.5 m (0.3 to 8.2 ft.), the robot is built for demanding material-handling tasks.

G2 Max’s force-controlled manipulation, omnidirectional mobility, and multiple safety features are intended to support efficient operations alongside existing industrial equipment and workflows.

The G2 Max industrial robot features dual-arm handling, force-controlled manipulation, and omnidirectional mobility for manufacturing and logistics applications. Source: AGIBOT

AGIBOT touts real-world deployments

To demonstrate how its G2 family performs in real operating environments, AGIBOT discussed deployments including tablet production, semiconductor packaging and testing, CNC machine tending, and logistics operations.

At computer maker Longcheer, robots are used in production-line material handling, where operating performance is assessed against cycle time, sustained operation and successful task completion. These are key performance indicators for manufacturing teams, said AGIBOT.

AGIBOT also presented G2 Max applications covering industrial material transport, warehouse handling, and pallet-related operations. These applications require more than a robot completing an isolated task: machines must operate safely around people and equipment, handle changes in the environment, and deliver consistent results over extended periods.

Beyond manufacturing, AGIBOT highlighted deployments in transportation and visitor-service environments, including Guangzhou Metro and the Chimelong tourism and entertainment complex. Robots perform tasks ranging from guiding visitors and answering questions to providing interactive services.

Unlike industrial handling, these applications place particular demands on speech comprehension, responsiveness, and sustained human-robot interaction. In this approach, AGIBOT asserted that deployment is not a one-off delivery milestone but an ongoing cycle of site integration, stable operation, and continuous improvement.

The company said the differences between factory and service work helps explain why Worken uses task-specific output benchmarks for different value. AGIBOT is using real deployment data and operating experience to explore how measures of autonomous working time and task output can be applied meaningfully in each setting.

Chuang Wang, partner, executive director, senior vice president, and president of the general-purpose humanoid business at AGIBOT, outlines the four capabilities behind scalable robot deployment: product readiness, manufacturing, on-site deployment, and ongoing operations. Source: AGIBOT

Link-U OS 1.0 part of wider AGIBOT open-source plans

AGIBOT officially released Link-U OS 1.0, which it claimed is “the industry’s first operating system purpose-built for embodied intelligence.” Built on a unified hardware abstraction layer, an embodied intelligence-native kernel, and a service framework, Link-U OS connects robot hardware with upper-layer applications.

The company is offering Link-U OS 1.0 as “a full-stack technology foundation spanning the entire process from development to deployment, and from underlying hardware enablement to upper-layer application support.”

The operating system has already been validated on mass-produced robots. Link-U OS 1.0 is currently being trialled by selected ecosystem partners, with plans for it to become fully open-source by the end of 2026.

AGIBOT also announced its OpenAtom Foundation Platinum Level Sponsorship and the donation of the Link-U OS project to the foundation. Through the OpenAtom Humanoid Community Joint Building Initiative, the two parties will jointly develop an open-source community for humanoid robots; promote unified technical interfaces and standards; and advance joint development, testing and validation, and talent training.

AGIBOT’s ecosystem now spans 255 universities, 511 enterprises, and more than 80,000 developers, supported by ongoing collaboration and research initiatives. The company said its partner and research ecosystem will extend deployment capabilities into additional scenarios and support repeatable implementation beyond individual pilots.

item.title: North American robot orders climb 24.8% in Q3 of 2026, says A3
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Robot demand from automotive component manufacturers nearly doubled in Q3, as other sectors posted strong gains, reported A3.

The post North American robot orders climb 24.8% in Q3 of 2026, says A3 appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
While automotive OEM orders declined in the first half of 2026, they picked up in Q3. Source: A3

North American companies ordered 10,989 robots valued at $723.5 million in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest data from the Association for Advancing Automation, or A3. Orders increased 24.8% in units and 26.1% in value compared with the third quarter of 2025, making it the strongest quarter of the year so far, it said.

The third-quarter gains pushed total orders for the first nine months of 2026 to 28,984 robots valued at approximately $1.89 billion, A3 reported. This represented increases of 9.6% in units and 13.3% in value over the same period last year, noted the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization.

Orders grow in automotive in addition to other industries

After declining during the first half of 2026, automotive OEM robot orders returned to positive year-over-year growth in the third quarter, increasing 7.5%, said A3. Orders from automotive component suppliers climbed 90.4%, continuing the strong demand from that segment seen earlier in the year.

Several other industries recorded substantial increases in robot orders during Q3:

  • Semiconductors and electronics/photonics: +97.6% units
  • Plastics and rubber: +67.7% units
  • Life sciences/pharmaceutical/biomedical: +38.7% units
  • Metals: +37.0% units

All other industries increased just 0.5% in units ordered, while food and consumer goods declined by 23.7%, A3 added.

The growth in the electronics segment occurred as investment grew in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, with strong demand for electronics supporting AI and other applications. Life sciences has also seen continued investment in domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing among others, said A3.

Automotive component orders were particularly strong despite earlier weakness among automotive manufacturing, said the organization. While OEM orders improved in Q3, they remained 17% below their year-earlier level through the first nine months of 2026.

“What stands out in the third quarter is not simply the magnitude of the growth, but how broadly it was distributed across the market,” stated Alex Shikany, executive vice president at A3. “Automotive OEM orders returned to positive growth, while automotive components and sectors such as semiconductors/electronics and life sciences posted significant gains. That broader mix is important because it points to a robotics market that is becoming increasingly diversified across industries and applications.”

Submit your innovation now!

Cobot orders increase 56%, finds A3

Force- and power-limited or collaborative robots also posted a strong third quarter, with 1,831 units valued at $63.8 million ordered. This was an increase of about 56% in units compared with Q3 2025. Collaborative robots accounted for 16.7% of all robot units ordered during the quarter.

Through September, North American companies ordered 4,605 cobots valued at approximately $178 million, representing 15.9% of total robot units and 9.4% of order value.

Collaborative robots continue to be used across a wide range of applications and industries. In the first nine months of 2026, cobots accounted for 43.8% of robot orders in life sciences/pharma/biomed and 36.9% in semi & electronics/photonics.

Manufacturing activity continues expansion

The stronger robot order numbers come alongside improving manufacturing activity, said A3. The September Institute of Supply Chain Management (ISM) Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) registered 54.5, marking a ninth consecutive month of expansion, while the Federal Reserve said that U.S. manufacturing output increasing 0.3% in September.

Higher input costs, trade uncertainty, and the timing of large manufacturing projects remain factors to watch, noted A3. “But with robot orders strengthening across several industries, the North American market enters the final quarter of 2026 with positive momentum,” it said.

More detailed Q3 2026 market data and graphs are available upon request for press and through the A3 Vault for member companies. A3 said it is the leading global advocate for the benefits of automating.

A3 has also expanded its Market Intelligence resources with “Business of Automation,” a weekly show examining industry developments; Business of Automation on Substack, offering additional analysis and industry updates; and SIGNAL, a free research series covering robotics, automation, and AI.

Association members seeking deeper insights can subscribe to MI+ for forecasts, detailed datasets, dashboards and industry analysis. A3 members represent more than 1,500 manufacturers, component suppliers, system integrators, end users, academic institutions, research groups, and consulting firms.

item.title: What Symbotic’s Walmart growth teaches robotics startups about anchor customers
item.dc:creator: Deepak Jayaraj
item.description:
Symbotic’s growth with Walmart shows how an anchor customer can fund a robotics startup’s scale while creating risks around customer concentration, contractual restrictions and the challenge of building a diversified, repeatable business.

The post What Symbotic’s Walmart growth teaches robotics startups about anchor customers appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Symbotic’s recent quarterly filing lists its largest customer, together with affiliates, as “Customer A,” and the annual report names that customer as Walmart. Customer A supplied 90.5% of revenue in the quarter that ended June 27, 2026. Symbotic reported $720.8 million in revenue and $55 million in net income for the same quarter.

Few robotics companies have turned one demanding customer into a business this size, and this profit follows earlier profits. The quarter also included $19.4 million of investment gains and negative non-GAAP free cash flow, so one quarter’s profit can’t settle whether leaning so heavily on Walmart has paid off.

For a startup founder deciding whether to sign a second customer soon, Walmart’s 90.5% share says little about the cost of serving another account. I’d look at how many people that account pulls into the field and what the contract obliges each side to do when plans change. I’d also ask how easily the anchor could get the same work done another way.

Walmart wrote its own insurance

Symbotic can’t afford to lose Walmart, and that dependence already gives the retailer some protection. Walmart’s contracts show that it didn’t rely on that incentive alone. The 2022 master automation agreement gives Walmart continuity rights, including the right to embed engineers with Symbotic and technical material held in escrow, which Walmart can use under specified conditions. The 2025 agreement for Walmart’s store-level Accelerated Pickup and Delivery (APD) systems repeats those protections. During the APD build-out, it also caps, at a redacted number, how many comparable APD systems Symbotic can sell to each outside customer every year. The filings don’t show whether Walmart has ever tested these rights, so they read more like preparation than a proven fallback.

When the APD deal closed in January 2025, Walmart committed $520 million of development funding. Symbotic paid Walmart a $200 million base price for its robotics business in the same transaction and agreed to two possible milestone payments of $175 million each. Symbotic gained funded development and the prospect of a large rollout, although the additional purchase commitment depends on performance milestones. In return, it accepted delivery obligations and limits on comparable APD sales to other customers.

Every new site borrows people

Operations-heavy robotics companies tend to add people as they add customers, at least until deployment becomes routine. Symbotic reported about 2,000 employees at the end of fiscal 2025, with roughly half working at customer sites to install, commission, and maintain its systems, and it brings in contractors as needed. Its standard model also has Symbotic operate a new system for a limited time before handing daily operation to the customer. Those field teams serve both new deployments and running systems, so the total can’t show what one more site would take. It does show how much of the business still happens where the robots are installed.

Where the newer Symbotic demand comes from

Symbotic has broadened its customer base, partly through structures it helped build. Exol, its warehouse-as-a-service venture with SoftBank, accounted for $11.6 billion of the $22.5 billion backlog at June 27, 2026, and Symbotic owns 35% of Exol and helps fund its build-out. Walmart de México, another newer customer, is majority-owned by Walmart. Exol lets customers use Symbotic’s system without buying it outright, and Walmex carries a proven relationship into a new market, so both routes make commercial sense. Both also move partly with decisions made by Symbotic or Walmart, so the longer customer list carries somewhat less independent demand than its length suggests.

Submit your innovation now!

A new Symbotic customer can take two years to go live

Symbotic’s management said in 2023 that it aimed to add one or two new customers a year. It has also described its historical timeline as about 24 months from a signed statement of work to acceptance. Medline signed in late fiscal 2025 and plans a pilot in 2027. Associated Wholesale Grocers announced a project in March 2026 and expects operations in the fourth quarter of 2027. Associated Food Stores announced its agreement in May 2023 and had its first phase running by February 2025.

Symbotic generally recognizes system revenue as it incurs costs, once acceptance is reasonably assured, so revenue can start before installation and well before go-live. The 24-month timeline instead shows how long a supplier can wait before a new customer’s site actually runs, which is when it learns whether the product traveled.

What I expect and what would change my mind

The scenario I would examine most closely has no villain. Walmart stays satisfied, meets its commitments, and finishes the distribution-center rollout on schedule. System revenue from that program then winds down, and the work that continues, mostly service and software, brings in less than installation did unless new system orders follow. The supplier did everything right, and its growth now depends on replacing a program that ended as planned. For Symbotic, the APD program and Exol are the obvious candidates to replace it, along with newer accounts, and I would watch whether they reach real scale before the distribution-center work tapers.

I expect Walmart to remain Symbotic’s dominant customer for years, and I’d be surprised to see its share fall below 80% before fiscal 2028. Walmart keeps expanding its own commitments, with the performance-dependent APD program added on top of the distribution-center rollout. New accounts tend to start with one site or a pilot, and management’s stated aim in 2023 was one or two new customers a year. Even with revenue recognized as costs are incurred, a single new site adds little next to dozens of Walmart projects moving at once. Exol is my largest uncertainty. Its revenue counts outside Walmart, so a faster build-out of its contracted systems could pull down Walmart’s reported share, even though I would still treat Exol separately when judging independent demand. A faster Exol ramp, or larger near-term rollouts by unrelated customers, would change my view.

I also expect strategic buyers to lean harder on contractual control. Protective terms of this kind already appear in automation contracts. I think buyers who invest in warehouse and humanoid startups, or deploy their robots at scale, will ask for them more often and in broader forms.

The same field-load logic explains why I expect a shakeout among humanoid pilots over the next few years. A pilot at one site with a few robots can run on subsidy. The robot maker’s engineers can install the robots, step in when one stalls, and absorb support costs that the pilot price doesn’t recover. A fleet contract tends to turn those hidden costs into obligations. When the buyer pays a fixed service price for uptime, extra interventions come out of the vendor’s margin. The humanoid companies that reach paid fleets will probably be the ones that used their pilots to measure and cut the field work each robot needs. A famous customer or a large funding round won’t guarantee that step. If several of these companies grow paid fleets and keep support costs predictable, I’d expect a milder shakeout than I do now.

What startups can take from Symbotic

Walmart got continuity rights and limits on Symbotic’s comparable sales in exchange for funding and scale. I think founders tend to judge an anchor deal by the size of the order and skim terms like these. A better habit is to go through the contract clause by clause and ask what each restriction costs in buyers the company can no longer pursue. The money deserves the same scrutiny, since every dollar comes with something to deliver or repay.

That funding goes furthest when it buys repeatability. Symbotic’s management has described moving testing to suppliers and standardizing build and test procedures, work that can pay off on every later deployment.

Startups do the same fieldwork with far fewer people. A second customer on the same system still pulls staff into the field, and one that needs a different integration pulls more of them, usually off the anchor’s rollout. Because the same small team tends to carry both jobs, a new logo can slow the anchor when it is paying the bills. As an operator, I would track field hours and unplanned engineering time across comparable deployments, the measure Symbotic’s filings can’t give outsiders. When design engineers keep getting pulled in to solve problems already solved at earlier sites, the product is still in development. It’s ready to scale once the team can predict and price the engineering and field work each new site requires.

Symbotic’s timeline is a reason to start testing with a second customer well before the anchor’s rollout slows. An early project with a defined scope and budget can show how much effort another account really takes. Rajat Bhageria of Chef Robotics has described combining multiple customers’ requirements into one product specification and charging modest non-recurring engineering fees before building. That way, several buyers shape one product without a one-off project for each. Adding accounts for revenue is a different decision, because it commits people. It belongs after the team can estimate what a new site takes and deliver it alongside existing projects.

Exol and Walmex also change how I would size a customer base. A buyer owned or funded by an existing partner tends to move with that partner, so independent budgets tell me more than the number of logos. AutoStore reached about 1,300 end customers through 23 distribution partners in fiscal 2025, yet four partners supplied 74% of its revenue. Concentration tends to move more easily than it disappears, so the real choice is which kind the company can survive.

Before hiring ahead of anchor demand, it pays to model two scenarios. One is a six-month pause in the rollout. The other is the rollout finishing on schedule, the no-villain case above, which tends to get left out of plans because it looks like success.

A Bossa Nova mobile shelf-scanning robot at work in a Walmart store. Source: Bossa Nova Robotics

What not to copy

The lesson I would leave behind is the concentration itself. Symbotic’s founder, Rick Cohen, also chairs C&S Wholesale Grocers, which gave Symbotic access to production environments during development, and Walmart later funded development directly. A startup whose anchor offers neither kind of support is making a different bet with the same percentage.

I’d also look at the financial strength of both the robotics company and the business supporting it. In agricultural robotics, Root AI became part of a grower when AppHarvest bought it in 2021. AppHarvest and its robotics subsidiary entered Chapter 11 in 2023, and the group’s court declaration pointed to farming losses and financing pressure. Zordi’s chief executive later announced that the company had bought AppHarvest’s robotics IP and assets, but the record doesn’t show whether Root AI could have stood on its own. Abundant Robotics shut down in 2021, a year in which its apple-growing partner, T&G Global, stayed profitable, and its chief executive said the company couldn’t raise enough investment to finish development. Root AI went down with its parent company, and Abundant ran out of investors before it could finish its harvester.

Walmart was also the main customer for Bossa Nova Robotics, a Carnegie Mellon spinout. By November 2020, Walmart had ended its relationship with the company, whose shelf-scanning robots had reached about 500 stores. Earlier that year, the companies had announced plans to reach 1,000 stores. The Wall Street Journal reported that employees picking online orders were giving Walmart another way to monitor inventory.

The Journal’s sources added that Walmart U.S. CEO John Furner had concerns about how shoppers reacted to robots in stores. One of them said Walmart told Bossa Nova it saw an improvement in stores with the robots, “but we don’t see enough of an improvement” in revenue and other metrics. Bossa Nova laid off about half its staff after the contract ended. It later shifted toward retail AI that could use images captured on phones, and the company eventually closed. I read Walmart’s decision as a reason to keep testing the customer’s alternatives as its operations change. A robot can keep doing its assigned job even as the customer finds less reason to pay for it.

Symbotic’s fiscal 2025 annual report says the contracts behind its backlog lack termination-for-convenience clauses. Most of that backlog can be terminated only for missed performance standards, insolvency, or specified changes in control. A founder can sort an anchor’s demand into orders the contract commits it to and expansion it can still walk away from. Hiring against that expansion means carrying those salaries if the orders don’t come, possibly for as long as it takes a new customer to go live.

About the author

Deepak Jayaraj is the vice president of hardware engineering and manufacturing at Four Growers, an agricultural robotics company based in Pittsburgh. With over 15 years of experience spanning space robotics, medical devices, and AgTech, he specializes in guiding robotics companies through the critical transition from prototype to scaled deployment and the economics of hardware business models.

item.title: Warp Sciences emerges from stealth, to apply robotics to drug research
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Warp Sciences has co-founders from OpenAI, Meta, and more, plus funding to build infrastructure for automated drug discovery in the U.S.

The post Warp Sciences emerges from stealth, to apply robotics to drug research appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Warp Sciences plans to create chemistry infrastructure for sovereign biotech. Source: deni AI, Adobe Stock

Warp Sciences last week emerged from stealth with $215 million in funding to create infrastructure that enables biotech and pharmaceutical companies to discover new medicines faster. The startup said it is building a U.S.-based chemistry contract research organization, or CRO, to bring together chemists, robotics, and AI to make and test molecules for research teams.

The South San Francisco-based company‘s stated goal is to provide experimental data to train better AI that in turn enables more capable labs, giving scientists the ability to test more ideas.

“AI has dramatically accelerated software engineering and mathematics, but it has yet to make the same impact in the physical sciences,” stated Kevin Weil, co-founder and CEO of Warp Sciences. “Chemistry and biology move forward when you make something, test it and learn from the result.”

“If we want to build more capable AI for science, we need to generate real-world data at scale,” he added. “Warp is starting that process by making the research compounds drug discovery needs today, while building the labs and automation to speed the cycle from hypothesis to experiment to answer.”

Warp said it has no proprietary drug pipeline itself; it is designing automated labs that can run experiments, learn from them, and improve with each cycle.

Warp Sciences focuses on sovereign biotechnology

A promising molecular design is only the beginning, observed Warp Sciences. “Scientists have to make it, test it, and use what they learn to decide what comes next,” said the company. “Faster access to compounds gives research teams faster answers, more ideas to pursue, and more opportunities to find medicines that change lives.”

Warp also noted the importance of sovereign biotechnology. In a 2024 survey by the Biotechnology Innovation Organization, 74% reported contracts with Chinese companies for preclinical and clinical services, according to Reuters. The BIOSECURE Act, signed into law in December 2025, established a framework for restrictions on federal procurement and funding involving designated biotechnology companies of concern.

In response, Warp claimed that it is building a U.S.-based chemistry partner that scientists can rely on for its speed, quality, and close collaboration. Its goal is to shorten the path from molecular design to testing while giving customers more control over where sensitive research takes place.

The company said its initial service will focus on lead optimization analog synthesis, making variations of molecules that scientists can compare as they search for a drug candidate. Experienced chemists will guide experiments as the lab is increasingly automated by robotics and AI, with AI models trained on data from physical experiments.

Warp plans to enable its customers to discover drugs more efficiently and keep that discovery in the U.S.

Submit your innovation now!

Founders’ expertise spans AI and healthcare

Warp Sciences noted that its founding team’s experience spans AI, data infrastructure, healthcare, and drug discovery. Weil most recently served as chief product officer and vice president of science at OpenAI. Chief Scientific Officer Solomon “Sol” Reisberg held medicinal chemistry leadership roles at Terremoto Biosciences.

“I’ve worked with overseas chemistry partners that delivered speed and value, but I still worried about protecting the intellectual property behind our programs,” said Reisberg. “We’re building Warp to give drug hunters that same caliber of chemistry services in the U.S., with IP protection at the center of the relationship, and without the price premium that U.S. boutique CROs currently demand.”

Chief Technology Officer “Manohar “Mano” Paluri was a vice president at Meta Superintelligence Labs and a founding member of FAIR. DJ Patil was a founding executive at Devoted Health and the first U.S. chief data scientist for the White House.

“Our goal is simple: Every experiment should make the next one smarter,” Paluri asserted. “AI needs a closer connection to the physical work of chemistry. Closing the loop between designing experiments, executing them, and learning from their outcomes builds increasingly capable systems for deciding what to make and how to make it. We’re building the software, AI and robotics alongside the lab so each part is shaped by what chemists actually need.”

Early hires have added robotics experience from companies including Genesis, Skild AI, and 1X Technologies, as well as scientific expertise from Genentech and Lawrence Livermore National Labs.

“Warp’s services bolster customer-led discovery programs. Our biotech and pharma customers determine which molecules to pursue and retain control of their drug programs,” said Patil. “We’re not developing drugs of our own. We’re building the infrastructure for the people who do.”

Venture capital firms, angel investors support Warp

Lightspeed led Warp Sciences’ funding, with participation from Premji Invest, Mayfield, IVP, Lux, Conviction, Menlo Ventures, 01 Advisors, Standard, Lowercarbon Capital, Gigascale Capital, Angular Ventures, Scribble Ventures, Uncork Capital, Innovation Endeavors, Matter VP, Zero Shot Fund, SignalFire and Moxxie Ventures.

Angel investors included Brian Armstrong (Coinbase CEO), Mike Krieger (Anthropic Labs co-lead, Instagram co-founder), Milan Kovac (former Tesla Robotics vice president), and Ion Stoica (Databricks co-founder). It also included Fidji Simo (former OpenAI AGI Deployment CEO), Brendan Foody (Mercor CEO), Mark Chen (OpenAI chief research officer), and Sarah Friar (OpenAI chief financial officer).

In addition, Kate Rouch (former OpenAI and Coinbase chief marketing officer), Lulu Meservey (Rostra CEO), Deepak Pathak (Skild AI CEO), Dylan Field (Figma CEO), and Lachy Groom (Physical Intelligence co-founder and chief operating officer) were angel investors.

item.title: WorldOracle Tests Whether World Models Can Reliably Predict Real-World Executions
item.dc:creator: Sponsored Content
item.description:
In one case showcased by WorldOracle, a robot's grasp missed, yet the world model predicted that the robot had successfully picked up the fruit.

The post WorldOracle Tests Whether World Models Can Reliably Predict Real-World Executions appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Key Takeaways

  • WorldOracle is a benchmark for action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) that scores each model’s predicted rollout against the paired real-world execution, with both starting from the same initial observations and following the same action sequence.
  • Seven representative models were evaluated; arm motion was predicted relatively well, but object positions and movements often deviated from reality, and performance dropped over complete operation sequences.
  • The platform opened to developers on October 16 and accepts both open-weight and closed-source models.

In one WorldOracle case, the robot’s grasp missed, yet the world model predicted a successful pick. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

In one case showcased by WorldOracle, a robot’s grasp missed, yet the world model predicted that the robot had successfully picked up the fruit.

Given the initial frame and action sequence of a real manipulation episode, the model generated a rollout that looked plausible on screen but differed from the actual execution. The success it depicted never happened in reality.

Researchers from Princeton University, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Toronto, NVIDIA and AgiBot have jointly introduced WorldOracle, a benchmark specifically designed to evaluate action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) by comparing their predictions with real-world executions that start from the same initial observations and follow the same action sequences.

The team evaluated seven representative models — among them DreamDojo, Cosmos 3, IRASim and GE-Sim 2.0 — and identified two prominent problems. First, while the motion paths of robot arms are predicted relatively well, the positions and movements of manipulated objects can still deviate from reality. Second, models that perform well over short horizons can degrade significantly over complete operation sequences.

On October 16, WorldOracle, an evaluation platform for action-conditioned world models, officially opened to developers. The research team has collected real manipulation episodes in advance, recording both video and actions. Developers use the initial frames and action sequences provided in the evaluation set to generate predicted videos and submit them to the platform, which scores each submission against the corresponding real execution record. The results show whether a model has accurately predicted the consequences of the actions, helping developers pinpoint weaknesses and verify improvements.

Project page: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18826

How Do Seven World Models Perform?
Arm motion is right, but objects don’t always follow

The predicted motion of a robot arm reaching toward a piece of fruit and closing its gripper may closely match its actual motion, yet the model can still incorrectly predict whether the fruit is lifted and where it moves next. To assess the two separately, the research team compared the position and motion of the robot arm and of the manipulated object in each predicted video against the real-world recording, and scored them individually.

Spatial alignment scores for the robot arm and the manipulated object. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

The results show that all five models evaluated on the human-operated AgiBot G2 data scored higher on the arm than on the object. In other words, even when the arm in the generated video follows the given actions well, the position and movement of the object may still depart from reality. IRASim scored 78.8 on the robot arm but only 29.1 on the manipulated object, while Cosmos 3 scored 89.4 and 45.4, respectively. The remaining models showed gaps of varying size.

Accuracy declines as the rollout horizon grows

Time presents a second challenge. Completing a continuous task often requires multiple grasps, placements and adjustments, and the object state left by one interaction becomes the starting point for the next. Whether a model stays close to reality must therefore be tested over the full process.

WorldOracle evaluates both the first 30 seconds of each trajectory and the complete long sequence.

WorldOracle-SV scores of the same models under the two evaluation horizons. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

On the same set of AgiBot G2 teleoperation data, the WorldOracle-SV scores of all five models fell. DreamDojo dropped from 50.56 to 27.08, and Cosmos 3 from 53.99 to 26.60, nearly halving in both cases. GE-Sim 2.0 fell from 73.86 to 63.33; it posted the highest score of the five models at both horizons and the smallest decline over the full sequence.

The relative ranking also shifted. IRASim scored below Ctrl-World, DreamDojo and Cosmos 3 over the first 30 seconds, but above all three over the full sequence.

What Can WorldOracle Measure?

WorldOracle evaluation framework: real actions are recorded, the model predicts what follows, and the result is scored against the real execution. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

Accurately predicting a failure earns a high score

WorldOracle starts from pre-collected records of real manipulation. A model is given the initial frame and the action sequence and generates a predicted video, which is compared with the real execution of the same actions.

What models must predict includes missed grasps, drops and spills. If an operation fails in reality, accurately predicting that failure counts as a correct prediction.

Failed executions therefore serve as an important class of test samples: they reveal whether a model follows the given actions and their consequences, or defaults to a successful version of the task.

The benchmark covers two robot embodiments, AgiBot G2 and YAM, as well as first-person human-hand manipulation. Four tasks (fruit picking, towel hanging, water pouring and drawer pulling) involve interaction with rigid, deformable, fluid and articulated objects, respectively. Task coverage varies by embodiment, as defined in the evaluation set.

The human-hand setting is intended for world models that can accept hand-motion input, testing whether a model can predict subsequent object changes and interaction outcomes from a recorded sequence of hand poses. Models with egocentric world-modeling capabilities are evaluated zero-shot in this setting, without any additional hand-adaptation data provided by the platform.

Real execution footage for the four task types. Credit: [WorldOracle team / AgiBot]

The data come from two sources. The first is human-operated data collection, including robot teleoperation trajectories and human hand-manipulation trajectories. The second is policy rollouts, in which an autonomous policy controls a real robot.

When a robot executes autonomously, it can produce pauses, jitter and motion corrections that differ from human operation. Including such data helps test whether a world model remains accurate when faced with actions from different sources.

The platform offers three tracks:

  • WorldOracle-Core: evaluates predictions over the first 30 seconds of human-operated trajectories.
  • WorldOracle-Policy: evaluates predictions over complete episodes of autonomous policy rollouts on AgiBot G2.
  • WorldOracle-Long: evaluates sustained prediction over complete, human-operated long sequences.

The WorldOracle study compares several embodied world-model benchmarks. Of these, WorldOracle is the only one that simultaneously covers action-sequence input, real-world execution data, failure cases, long-horizon interaction, multiple embodiments, multi-view evaluation and autonomous policy rollouts.

Breaking down prediction error: outcomes and process

The predicted and real robot arm positions may closely match even when the model gets the fruit’s grasp state wrong; two final states may look alike while the paths that led to them differ. A single score can hardly capture such differences.

WorldOracle checks predictions with four complementary metrics:

  • Physical State Correctness: checks whether object positions, grasp states and liquid transfer at the end of each interaction match the real outcome.
  • Interaction Spatial Alignment: checks whether the positions and movement paths of objects, robot arms or human hands are consistent with the real process.
  • Key Interaction Area Fidelity: focuses on regions such as the object, gripper and hand, combining pixel-level, perceptual and semantic similarity to reduce the influence of large background areas on the score.
  • Multi-View Action Coherence: for models that support multi-view output, checks whether robot motion across synchronized camera views is aligned with the real execution.

The first three metrics are averaged with equal weights to form the WorldOracle-SV (single-view) score; for multi-view evaluation, the fourth metric is added and the four are again equally weighted. Sub-scores are also retained, allowing developers to distinguish problems in state prediction, motion trajectories and local detail.

To validate the metrics, the researchers asked 119 participants to compare 128 pairs of predicted videos. The four metrics agreed with human choices on which prediction was better 88.1% to 93.2% of the time.

The researchers also note the benchmark’s limits. It measures how closely a prediction matches a single recorded real execution. For fluids, deformable objects and stochastic contact, the same action can lead to several plausible outcomes, and a single reference cannot fully describe that range.

Training support also differs across embodiments: AgiBot G2 models use a benchmark-specific training set, YAM models use public data, and the human-hand setting is evaluated zero-shot. Scores across the three settings should therefore not be used directly to judge embodiment difficulty or cross-embodiment generalization.

How Can Developers Participate?
Open submissions give model iteration concrete feedback

WorldOracle supports both open-weight and closed-source models. After registration and approval, developers choose a track according to the embodiment or manipulation setting their model supports, generate and upload predicted videos following the submission guide, and view composite scores, sub-scores and comparisons.

For model iteration, this feedback can be tied to specific questions: Did a change make object motion more accurate? Did it reduce incorrect predictions of failed operations? Does the improvement still hold as the prediction horizon grows?

Whether the futures generated by a world model can be relied upon must be tested against real execution. WorldOracle turns that test into a unified set of tasks, data and scoring methods, giving developers a basis for comparing models, identifying errors and verifying improvements.

Project page: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/

Submission guide: https://worldoracle-benchmark.github.io/submission/

Sponsored content by WorldOracle

The post WorldOracle Tests Whether World Models Can Reliably Predict Real-World Executions appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: ANYbotics begins delivering ANYmal X legged robot for explosive atmospheres
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
ANYbotics has designed the ANYmal X inspection robot to comply with the strictest safety standards of the oil, gas, and chemical industries.

The post ANYbotics begins delivering ANYmal X legged robot for explosive atmospheres appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
ANYmal X is certified to operate in hazardous atmospheres. Source: ANYbotics

Hazardous environments are good use cases for robots, which are expanding into new use cases. ANYbotics AG today launched ANYmal X, which it claimed is “the world’s first legged inspection robot for explosive atmospheres.”

The new quadruped is designed to meet strict safety standards in oil, gas, and chemicals, said the company. ANYmal X uses an advanced industrial AI stack to conduct routine autonomous inspections in environments that are dangerous to people, it said.

“Four years of pioneering engineering with more than 10 patents went into ANYmal X,” stated Péter Fankhauser, co-founder and CEO of ANYbotics. “Many experts thought a legged robot could never be made safe for explosive atmospheres.

“Oil, gas and chemical plants are among the most hazardous and most costly places to operate,” he added. “That makes them the prime case for physical and industrial AI, yet until now, the areas that matter most were off-limits to robots like ours. That changes today.”

Spun out of ETH Zurich in 2016, ANYbotics said its ANYmal robots and the Shift operations platform automate routine inspections in multiple industries, keeping people out of harm’s way and turning inspection data into maintenance action. Backed by more than $150 million from leading European and Silicon Valley investors, ANYbotics has about 200 employees in Zurich, San Francisco, and Barcelona.

Equipment failures in hazardous spaces are costly, says ANYbotics

“Valued at $102 billion, the global oil, gas, and chemical sector is the largest market for autonomous inspection,” noted ANYbotics. “Two major operational costs drive this market value: the expensive skilled labor required for manual inspection, and the downtime caused by preventable equipment failures.”

“Because critical components, like pumps, compressors, valves, and piping, are located in hazardous zones, where standard robots are banned, human operators still need personal protective equipment, handheld gas detectors, and entry permits to inspect these areas on foot,” it said.

Undetected equipment failures cost the world’s 500 largest companies roughly $1.4 trillion each year in preventable downtime, ANYbotics said. In the oil and gas sector alone, a single hour of unplanned downtime can cost up to $500,000 according to Siemens, while U.S. extraction workers face a fatality rate seven times the national average, found NIOSH.

In addition to keeping workers out of harm’s way and minimizing downtime, ANYmal X can provide continuous, repeatable, structured observational data that enhances digital facility planning models, such as digital twins. ANYbotics said this gives them greater contextual detail to be more useful across an entire organization.

Submit your innovation now!

Certifying a robot for hazardous zones is one of the hardest parts of the design process

Every device used in hazardous areas, from radios to flashlights, must be explosion-protected, or “ex-proof,” said ANYbotics. Each unit requires independent certification proving it cannot ignite a flammable atmosphere, even when something fails. ANYbotics built ANYmal X to comply with the ATEX standard in Europe and IECEx globally.

Fixed equipment typically achieves compliance using heavy, explosion-proof enclosures or limiting electrical energy to prevent ignition, the company explained. A legged robot cannot use either approach. It requires high-power motors and a large battery in a frame light enough to climb stairs, exposed cameras and sensors for navigation, and autonomous docking capabilities.

ANYbotics has designed its legged robots for complex environments. Source: ANYbotics

Every one of these components had to be certified ex-proof without sacrificing the autonomous mobile robot’s (AMR) payload capacity, agility, or operating speed, said ANYbotics.

“We asked one question over and over: Which credible event in the life of a walking robot could create an ignition source, and how do we make sure it never does?” said Andrea Corda, chief technology officer of ANYbotics. “Working closely with the certification bodies, we answered that question component by component. The result is a new explosion-protection approach for an entire class of autonomous mobile robots.”

ANYbotics performed a comprehensive ignition-risk assessment for ANYmal X’s service life and implemented safeguards for each potential ignition source. Each of its components has been designed to minimize ignition risk.

The company said the new robot’s AI computer and inspection equipment are enclosed in nitrogen-filled, sealed chambers. Non-metallic shells insulate metallic components, conductive feet provide grounding, and automatic cutoffs monitor temperature. All 12 leg actuators and its battery are protected by flameproof casings. Charging and data transmission use energy barriers, so no connection is exposed to hazardous areas.

ANYmal X’s onboard software monitors the robot’s condition before, during, and after each mission. It also tests durability against shock, vibration, corrosion, solar radiation, and salt mist to ensure that all protective measures function properly in normal use.

ANYmal X ships as a ‘complete system’ proven at industrial scale

“A certified robot is only the entry ticket for inspecting oil, gas, and chemicals facilities,” said Thierry Obédé, chief revenue officer at ANYbotics. “ANYmal X is a complete end-to-end inspection solution built for performance, safety, and security. It combines autonomous navigation, industrial AI for data interpretation, and integrations that convert findings directly into maintenance work orders.”

“Today, more than 50 power, metals, and materials customers use this system to run over 120,000 autonomous inspections every month,” he added.

ANYmal X runs on Shift, which schedules robot missions, organizes findings by asset, and helps maintenance teams track changes over time. It connects inspection findings with existing plant maintenance software, including SAP, Yokogawa, and SLB. To ensure top-tier data protection, the whole system is developed and operated under ISO 27001 information security standards.

“Plants run on process data from their control systems and business data from their ERP,” said Obédé. “The third source, what operators see, hear and measure on their rounds, has always been manual. ANYmal X now captures it autonomously, even inside hazardous areas, and we stand behind the whole chain, from the robot on site to the work order in the maintenance system.”

The ANYmal X robot autonomously conducts industrial inspections. Source: ANYbotics

Industry leaders tested ANYmal X

Since 2023, energy and chemical leaders including BP, Equinor, Shell, PETRONAS, Petrobras, BASF, and SLB have tested ANYmal X across hundreds of onshore and offshore missions through ANYbotics’ Early Access Program. Their feedback helped to refine the field-tested, industrial-grade robot now being delivered to customers.

ANYmal X does not require any facility modifications, navigating complex industrial environments such as steep stairs and narrow walkways, said ANYbotics.

The robot’s integrated thermal, visual, acoustic, and gas sensors detect overheating, leaks, abnormal noise, and equipment wear, logging every reading directly to its corresponding asset, the company said. This gives reliability engineers a standardized baseline to track asset health over time, enabling teams to spot early signs of wear and intervene before minor issues escalate into costly plant shutdowns.

ANYmal X and its full industrial AI stack will be shown publicly for the first time at ADIPEC 2026 by ANYbotics, SLB, and Kuwait Oil Co.

The post ANYbotics begins delivering ANYmal X legged robot for explosive atmospheres appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Embotech and BMW move 1M vehicles with automated driving technology
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
Embotech is automatically moving 3,500 vehicles around the clock daily across four BMW sites in the U.K. and Germany.

The post Embotech and BMW move 1M vehicles with automated driving technology appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
A MINI autonomously rolls off a U.K. production line using Embotech technology. Source: BMW Group

As vehicles come off the production line, human drivers typically need to get into each one to drive them to be parked or loaded onto trucks. Embotech and BMW today said they have moved 1 million vehicles using Embotech’s automated driving technology across four sites in the U.K. and Germany.

“Automated vehicle movements only create value when intelligence, safety, and reliability come together,” stated Andreas Kyrtatos, CEO of Embotech. “This milestone shows what is possible when proven technology is integrated into live production and operated reliably around the clock.”

Spun out of ETH Zurich in 2013, Embotech claimed that it is a global leader in safety-certified SAE Level 4 autonomous driving systems for industrial logistics and the first company worldwide to hold multiple TÜV-certified Level 4 solutions. Its two certified systems – Automated Vehicle Marshalling (AVM) and Autonomous Tractor Solution (ATS) – are built on a shared platform and are deployed in automotive factories, vehicle distribution centers, ports, and logistics yards.

The Zurich-based company said its technology can improve safety, productivity, resilience, and sustainability across logistics operations. In July, Embotech entered a strategic partnership with HTEC to scale deployment of autonomous driving across vehicles, customer programs, and industrial sites.

Submit your innovation now!

Embotech helps automaker increase flexibility

While automotive OEMs are already major users of industrial automation, they are continuing to digitize and adopt new technologies to make production processes more efficient, noted Embotech. However, much of the market remains at the pilot stage, autonomously operating only a limited number of vehicles, it said.

The Automated Driving In-Plant is vehicle- and OEM-agnostic and connects to existing drive-by-wire capabilities.

“Perception for [AVM] is in the infrastructure — vehicles don’t need self-driving capabilities or extra sensors,” Eva Beck, chief commercial officer at Embotech, told The Robot Report. “Hesai lidars are mounted in the production environment, so there are no hardware modifications. In the factory, we have a standardized software interface, offboard computers, and servers that optimize driving trajectories 10 times per second.”

Embotech provides key components, including its AI-based software for perception, prediction, and planning, which enables vehicles to operate in complex industrial environments. They also include a separate, deterministic architecture, independently certified by TÜV SÜD, that defines and enforces the safety boundary.

“Safety is one of the main motivations of the OEMs, as is reducing manual errors or damage caused by manual behavior,” explained Beck. “Vehicle movements need to be precise and to integrate into OEM space constraints. Our system can work alongside factory workers and manually driven vehicles. This enables us to integrate into existing processes and work in all weather conditions.”

A fleet manager gets destinations from the OEM’s back-end systems, defines vehicle routes, and manages communications among automated vehicles, she said.

The value for manufacturers goes beyond individual vehicles, asserted Embotech. Automated movements can support smoother vehicle flow, more stable and flexible operations, and round-the-clock capability independent of shift staffing.

BMW scales from pilot to network deployment

“The 1 million vehicle milestone demonstrates the scale that BMW Group has achieved with Automated Driving In-Plant, spanning different sites, brands, vehicle types, and production and logistics processes,” said Embotech. The partners added that they have demonstrated that the system is precise and reliable enough to scale within BMW‘s live production network.

BMW and Embotech have brought the Automated Driving In-Plant system to about 3,500 vehicle movements a day, with more than 99.5% availability. In manufacturing environments where unexpected downtime can disrupt wider operations, maintaining that level of availability is essential to keeping automated vehicle movements integrated, said Embotech.

Since an initial pilot in 2022, Embotech deployments have expanded to four BMW sites including Dingolfing, Leipzig, and Regensburg in Germany and MINI Plant Oxford in the U.K. The technology supports different use cases in defined production and logistics areas in each factory.

“One million vehicles moved using automated driving technology and the deployment of this technology at four sites to date demonstrates the innovative strength and scaling capabilities of our production network,” said Raymond Wittmann, the member of BMW AG’s board responsible for production. “We recognized the potential of Automated Driving In-Plant early, tested it in a pilot phase, and systematically developed it to series maturity. We are now rolling out this technology worldwide.

“Automated Driving In-Plant is a prime example of how we are translating the vision of the BMW iFACTORY into industrial practice and driving the efficiency, digitalization and intelligent connectivity across our production,” he added.

Embotech said its Munich team has worked closely with BMW to develop supporting tools and processes for deployment, monitoring, diagnosis, and recovery. “Operational experience supports the continuous improvement of Embotech’s perception, prediction, and planning software, helping future deployments and software releases build on what has been learned in live production,” it said.

“What excites us over and above the 1 million milestone is the pace at which that experience is compounding,” said Kyrtatos. “With BMW Group, we completed the first 500,000 automated vehicle movements in 15 months and the next 500,000 in just seven. For Embotech, the next phase is about taking what we have learned into more use cases, sites, customers, and industrial environments.”

“We’re also looking to roll out Automated Driving In-Plant next year at BMW Spartanburg,” Beck said, referring to the South Carolina factory where BMW has tested Figure AI humanoid robots. “We are scaling our solution further across use cases and customers.”

item.title: Xpanner launches autonomous pile driver for solar farm contruction
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Xpanner's new X1 Piling R6 robot autonomously drives solar posts with one operator, improving placement accuracy while cutting on-site labor.

The post Xpanner launches autonomous pile driver for solar farm contruction appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The Xpanner X1 Piling R6 is an automated pile-driving system for utility-scale solar and battery energy storage sites. | Credit: Xpanner

Xpanner today announced the X1 Piling R6, a fully automated pile-driving robot built to autonomously install posts for utility-scale solar and battery energy storage, or BESS, sites. Supervised by a single operator, the system uses high-precision GNSS and onboard sensors to place each pile accurately, helping builders keep pace with new power demand despite a shortage of skilled crews.

The core of the robot is Xpanner’s Everstar R6 crawler base machine. The R6 is equipped with the Santa Fe Springs, Calif.-based company‘s automation stack with onboard sensors and controls to autonomously complete the pile driving process for each post.

Xpanner designs for simplified operation

An operator uploads a plan, then walks X1 Piling R6 machine to the row using a remote control interface. The operator supervises the construction as the machine drives each pile accurately.

The R6 can autonomously navigate to the subsequent pile locations using high-precision GNSS antennas and receivers, precision sensors, and the Xpanner-developed automation controller. One operator can remotely manage the installation process.

“Solar and BESS builders are racing to bring new power online for the grid and for AI data centers, and they can’t find enough skilled crews to keep up,” said Henri Lee, co-founder and CEO of Xpanner. “X1 lets one operator drive every pile plumb with a single touch, keeps people away from the mast, and logs each pile as it goes in. It takes the automation EPCs [engineering, procurement, and construction firms] already trust on PD10 and puts it on a more powerful, more versatile machine.”

X1 connects to Xpanner Connect, the company’s web-based project dashboard. Project teams can load the pile schedule and coordinates, assign machines, and set up a site in minutes.

As X1 works, it records each pile’s position, depth, and plumb and posts it to a live project map, replacing manual counts, phone calls, spreadsheets, and end-of-day reports. Managers can also monitor machine state, cycle counts, and alerts across the fleet without a site visit.

Xpanner said business model is a mixed capex/SaaS subscription model. Customers purchase (or rent) the X1 Piling robot and then license the automation software on a monthly subscription basis for each active technology.

According to the company, the subscription is not tied to a specific project, site, or number of piles driven. Rather, the customer pays for the technology while it is actively being used. Once piling operations or the applicable task is completed, the equipment and technology can be transferred to another project and activated as needed.

Xpanner handles initial installation, calibration, operator training, and technical support, while the contractor provides the equipment operators on-site.

The Xpanner X1 Piling robot autonomously installs the posts for a solar panel farm. | Credit: Xpanner

Key features of the X1 Piling R6 robot

  • Power for hard ground: The system includes a 97 kW (130 hp) engine and a high-frequency hydraulic hammer with up to 1,260 J (929 ft.-lb.) of impact energy and three energy settings to match soil conditions.
  • Fine positioning without tramming: The guide rail slides 11.8 in. (300 mm) forward and back and 19.7 in. (500 mm) left and right, and the upper body rotates 180 degrees, putting the hammer on target from a single setup.
  • Range of pile lengths: The X1 can drive piles up to 23 ft. (7.0 m) long, with a maximum driving depth of 15.7 ft. (4.8 m). Because the hammer lowers near the ground and piles can be driven flush to grade, one machine handles standard tracker piles, short motor piles, and BESS foundation piles without an adapter.
  • Built for the field: Features include a mast that does not need disassembly for transport, a large fuel tank for long shifts, engine auto-idle, a large-capacity cooler, manual override, and e-stop.
  • Multi-function mast (and potential capabilities): DTH drilling, auger drilling, and ground screwing on the same carrier, so one machine can pre-drill and drive.

The X1 Piling R6 is designed to work together with the X1 panel lift, which was released earlier this year, for autonomous solar panel installation.

The post Xpanner launches autonomous pile driver for solar farm contruction appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Bedrock Robotics nears $1B in total funding as demand for autonomous heavy equipment surges
item.dc:creator: Mike Oitzman
item.description:
Bedrock Robotics has secured $600 million to scale autonomous heavy equipment and combat construction labor shortages.

The post Bedrock Robotics nears $1B in total funding as demand for autonomous heavy equipment surges appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Bedrock Robotics automates large excavators to improve construction site economics. | Credit: Bedrock Robotics

San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics has raised $600 million in Series C funding, co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, at a $4.1 billion valuation. The round brings its total funding to nearly $1 billion as it scales fully autonomous heavy equipment to address nationwide construction labor shortages.

The round included new investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, NVIDIA, and others. Bedrock said this will accelerate the deployment of Bedrock-equipped machines across commercial construction sites across the U.S., helping contractors use existing heavy equipment more safely, predictably, and at greater capacity.

The new capital follows a rapid commercial expansion beyond the company’s initial footprint in the West and Central South into the Midwest and South Atlantic. Anchored by a major partnership with Southwest contractor Haydon to automate earthwork in Texas, Bedrock has added regional partners across Minnesota, Florida, Georgia, Missouri, and Virginia—pushing its autonomous retrofits onto live job sites spanning data centers, healthcare facilities, and heavy civil infrastructure.

“We have proven that fully autonomous excavators can perform real work of value alongside the crews and workflows already in place on job sites,” said Boris Sofman, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Robotics. “The next challenge is delivering that capability to more contractors as a dependable part of how projects get built.”

“This funding allows us to expand deployments, strengthen the field operations behind every machine, and work with more partners as they integrate intelligent systems into everyday work,” he added. “The opportunity is to help the industry’s experienced crews safely take on more projects, deliver with greater consistency, and quickly deliver more of the infrastructure this country needs.”

Sofman told The Robot Report, “New customer demand is very high. We’re responsibly growing into the demand, bringing on new customers we can serve alongside our longtime design partners. We’re scaling across the board, from operations to hardware to supply chain operations, to keep pace with the needs of our customers.”

Bedrock Robotics adds leadership

In the midst of securing new funding, the company also added two new individuals to the management team.

Amy Jones Satrom joins the leadership team as vice president of operations. She brings operations experience from Amazon, Nuro, and Uber to lead the company in the next phase of scaling to meet demand.

“Amy is instrumental in strengthening our operations and building the systems and support that make successful deployments repeatable,” according to Sofman. “She’s still early in her tenure, but her leadership will be central to growing our deployment and production teams and preparing them to support customers across the country.

“Ajay Gummalla, a co-founder and VP of engineering, is also intimately involved on the hardware side of things, adding resilience to our supply chain so we’re ready to build the hardware we need to meet customer demand,” he explained.

Lando Juarez has joined Bedrock Robotics in the role of general counsel. He was formerly head of legal for Uber’s Autonomous Mobility & Delivery business, overseeing commercial partnerships and regulatory pathways.

Submit your innovation now!

Looking to the future of construction

When asked bout how the company is planning to grow, Sofman responded, “Short term, our growth market remains construction. It is a massive market — 4% to 5% of U.S. GDP — so we’re thinking about expanding use cases. Haydon will test our excavators for autonomous trench work.”

“We’re also thinking about automating larger machine models — Haydon and others will explore bulldozers, ADTs, and wheel loaders as possible heavy machines to automate next,” he said. “Long term: We’re looking at the other industries, like mining and agriculture, that are 1) also dealing with labor constraints and 2) use the same kinds of heavy machines GCs do.”

“For 2027, we are relentlessly focused on getting more Bedrock-equipped machines on more job sites around the country,” Sofman continued. “It was just a few months ago that we first launched fully autonomous excavators on live, commercial job sites, just two years after Bedrock came out of stealth. 2027 is about doubling down on that progress, getting to triple-digit machines working autonomously across the country.”

When asked about the installed base and economic opportunity for Bedrock Robotics’ systems, Sofman was more reserved.

“It’s a bit early to give concrete numbers,” said Sofman, “However, given the labor constraints on general contractors, the math pencils out: Imagine a job that can be completed two months faster because autonomous machines are running around the clock, seven days a week.”

“The developer paying 9% interest on a $400 million loan would save $6 million on that project they can invest into future projects,” he observed. “In turn, construction crews and all the downstream trades, like plumbing and electrical, would see an increasing volume of steady work because there are more projects that can be funded.”

Some data on labor constraints that have opened the market for Bedrock:

  • Twenty percent of construction workers are over the age of 55, and estimates suggest that more than 40% of the construction workers will retire in the next five years.

  • Large projects already run an average of 20% over schedule and 80% over budget.

  • In construction specifically, 87% of firms report openings for hourly craft positions, and 88% say the roles are as hard or harder to fill than a year ago.
